## Summary
Lenses checked: correctness, silent-failure, tests, comments.
`m0003_drop_legacy_email` must back up `users` before it drops `legacy_email`, because without that backup the drop permanently deletes production data and nothing can restore it.

## Changes
The pull request adds migration `m0003`, which drops `users.legacy_email`, and migration `m0004`, which backs up `orders` and then drops `orders.coupon_code`. It also adds one test that runs migrations m0001 through m0004 in order.

## Critical
- migrations/m0003_drop_legacy_email.py:7 — correctness — Call backup_table before dropping legacy_email — When this runs against a `users` table that has rows, `ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN legacy_email` deletes every `legacy_email` value and writes no `users_backup_3` copy first. `migrations/safety.py:3-5` says every destructive migration calls `backup_table` first because a deploy rollback cannot undo a dropped column, and `m0002`:7 and `m0004`:7 both do this. — If the deploy is rolled back or the column turns out to be needed after all, every user's legacy_email is lost and `restore_table` has nothing to restore. — Fix: Import `backup_table` from `migrations.safety` and call `backup_table(conn, "users", VERSION)` before the drop, as `migrations/m0002_drop_nickname.py:7` does, then extend `test_drop_retired_columns` to insert a user row and check `users_backup_3`.
